fields.title: Soyka: Not Enough Traffic for an A/B Test
fields.summary: The team insists on testing everything with A/B experiments, but there are only three hundred clients. Decide how to validate changes.
fields.decisionPrompt: How will you validate this change and product changes in general?
fields.brief/role: You are the product manager at Soyka.
fields.brief/company: Soyka is a fictional case management system for law firms: 300 clients, about 4,200 users, subscription starting at 12 thousand rubles a month.
fields.brief/context: The new Head of Product demands that every change go through an A/B test: 'like in normal companies'. The next change is a redesign of the case file, where lawyers currently waste time. The team has been arguing for three weeks, and work is stalled.
fields.brief/objective: Decide how to validate changes in this product.
fields.brief/constraints: One sprint cycle is two weeks. Interface updates are visible to all employees in a firm simultaneously: accounts are shared within each firm.
fields.brief/task: Choose a validation approach and justify it.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: A/B testing is not synonymous with validation
fields.learnTakeaway/body: A statistical test requires a sufficient number of independent units; where you have three hundred clients working in teams, it won't yield an honest answer. That is no reason to rely on gut feel: rolling out to a small cohort with predefined criteria, observing real usage, and validating specific risks separately yields a verifiable decision. The mistake isn't picking the tool, but applying it without doing the math.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
300 client firms, 4,200 users, with about 1,900 daily active users.

A case file is opened 24 times a day per lawyer on average.

Target metric: time spent adding a case event, currently averaging 3 minutes 40 seconds.

Expected improvement estimated by the team: about 20%.

With 1,900 active users and an effect that large, a user-level test would reach statistical significance in about a week — but users inside a firm collaborate and discuss UI changes, so they cannot be considered independent.

If randomized by firm, there are only 300 units, and variance between firms is larger than the expected effect: large firms average 5 minutes, small ones 2 minutes.

Annual churn: 9 firms. Testing the impact on churn in an A/B test is mathematically impossible.
fields.evidenceCards/1/title: How changes were tested until now
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
For two years, changes were shipped to everyone at once, followed by a before-and-after comparison.

Last year, search optimization was 'validated' this way: search time dropped by 30%. Later it turned out two large firms with the biggest case loads churned that month, dropping the average due to cohort shift.

There is a group of 11 firms willing to try changes early: the team calls them, and they give feedback willingly. Formally not a representative sample, but they vary in size.

No records of past tests exist: decisions were discussed in meetings.

Support tickets show 'adding a case event' has been the top complaint for two consecutive years, with 214 tickets in six months.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
Current flow for adding an event: open case → 'Events' tab → 'Add' button → 9-field form (4 required) → save → return to list.

Proposed change: quick 3-field form embedded directly in the case file, remaining fields optional.

Risk raised by lawyers during the last meeting: if optional fields are skipped, court reports will have to be compiled manually. Two lawyers said that would be worse than a slow form.

Engineering estimate: three weeks.

Rollback takes one day, no data is overwritten.

Enabling for a subset of firms is technically feasible.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
The Head of Product came from a company with 12 million users and insists on A/B testing as the standard.

The Chief Revenue Officer thinks testing is a waste of time: 'just ask clients, they will tell you'.

Sales promised three large accounts 'faster case processing this half-year'.

The engineering team has been waiting three weeks for a decision, doing minor fixes in the meantime.

Last quarter, two changes shipped without validation: one stuck, the other was reverted after a month due to complaints, without ever pinpointing the root cause.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Acknowledge that A/B testing won't work here and validate differently
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Use numbers to show why an A/B test won't yield answers, roll out to an early-adopter cohort with pre-defined criteria and active observation, validate the reporting risk separately, and record the findings.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
Calculations take an hour and settle the argument: 300 firms with variance from 2 to 5 minutes won't yield statistical significance for a 20% effect, and splitting within a firm is invalid because colleagues sit together.
Instead of an A/B test, roll out to 11 early firms for three weeks with pre-defined criteria: average time to add an event drops below 3 minutes, zero complaints regarding court reports, and at least four out of eleven firms keep using the quick form in week three.
Observing two lawyers live reveals what metrics wouldn't show: they use the quick form for routine events and switch to the full form for court hearings — which is expected behavior.
The court report risk is addressed separately: optional fields are highlighted when generating reports, not during data entry.
You log the result as a knowledge card, including boundaries: 'not validated on large firms, as only two were in the pilot'.
Trade-off: this does not yield a p-value, and you had to explain to the Head of Product why his standard framework doesn't apply here.
fields.decisionOptions/1/label: Run an A/B test anyway and wait longer
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: The Head of Product is right that data beats opinion. Split firms 50/50 and wait until statistical significance is reached.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
The test runs for eight weeks. Variance across firms exceeds the effect size, leaving a wide confidence interval: 'somewhere between −5% and +25%'.
During this time, two test-group firms complain that their interface differs from colleagues at other firms — shared accounts and networking made the difference obvious.
Ultimately, the decision is made via debate anyway, just two months late and with eroded trust.
The sales promise to three key accounts is missed.
Trade-off: an experiment tool was applied where sufficient data doesn't exist; lack of statistical significance was mistaken for lack of impact.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Ship to everyone and compare before vs after
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: This is how things were done for two years. Ship, check average event logging time before vs after, revert if metrics worsen.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
The change ships quickly, which is its only virtue.
Average time drops by 26% — a great headline number. But four small firms onboarded that same month with times naturally twice as fast, accounting for part of the drop.
This exact scenario happened a year ago with search optimization when two large firms churned.
In week five, a major firm files a complaint about court reports — a risk warned about upfront, now magnified across the entire customer base.
Trade-off: speed came at the expense of causal understanding; the metric cannot be trusted or documented honestly.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Survey clients and build according to survey results
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: The CRO is right: there aren't many clients and they are accessible. Send a survey about the new form and follow the majority.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The survey yields 74 responses. 68% respond that they need a quick form — predictable, because the question essentially reads 'do you want things faster?'.
Meanwhile, two lawyers who warned about court reporting issues also answered 'yes' on the survey: the risk didn't surface in a questionnaire.
After launch, the same complaint about manual court reports comes in, undetected by survey metrics.
Trade-off: stated intent was measured instead of actual behavior; customer conversations were appropriate here, but as user observation rather than a voting exercise.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Comparing hypotheses by appeal rather than reach, impact, and verification cost
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Setting experiment rules after looking at the numbers
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Failing to turn results into documented knowledge with clear boundaries
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Roadmap looks like a timeline of features instead of problems and metrics
